summary: Specifies IPv4 service continuity requirements for IPv6 customer edge routers, whether supplied by the provider or sold at retail. It extends the base requirements in RFC 7084 to allow IPv6 transition services for IPv4-as-a-Service. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Home routers in IPv6-only networks still need to let old IPv4 sites work. This document lists what such a router must be able to do.

questions: ipv4 as a service cpe requirements
how do home routers support ipv4 in ipv6-only networks
subtitle: Requirements for IPv6 routers to deliver IPv4 services through transition mechanisms.

tldr.problem: IPv6-only networks still need to support legacy IPv4 applications and services, but routers must know which transition mechanisms to support and how to configure them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8585 extends RFC 7084 with requirements for IPv6 customer edge routers to support five specific transition technologies: 464XLAT, DS-Lite, Lightweight 4over6, MAP-E, and MAP-T, along with configuration and multicast support.
tldr.outcome: Residential and small business routers can now transparently deliver IPv4 services to local networks connected to IPv6-only providers, enabling a gradual transition to IPv6.

facts.label: Target devices
facts.value: Residential, SOHO, and small enterprise routers

today: RFC 8585 is an Informational RFC published in May 2019. These requirements are now reflected in router implementations from major vendors, enabling seamless IPv4 service in IPv6-only networks. Service providers deploying IPv6-only access use these mechanisms to maintain IPv4 compatibility while managing the transition.

sections.title: The Problem: IPv6-Only Networks
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are running out. Rather than give every device an IPv4 address, internet service providers are deploying IPv6-only networks, where the connection from your home to the ISP uses only IPv6. However, many devices and services on the internet still use only IPv4. A home router in an IPv6-only network must bridge this gap, delivering IPv4 service continuity so that both IPv4-only and IPv6-only devices in the home can reach IPv4-only services on the internet.

RFC 7084 defined basic requirements for IPv6 customer edge routers. RFC 8585 extends those requirements to mandate support for IPv4-as-a-Service mechanisms that enable this transition.
sections.eli5: The internet is switching from IPv4 to IPv6, but many old websites and devices still only speak IPv4. A home router needs to be smart enough to translate between them so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Network Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture involves three layers: the service provider's IPv6-only WAN (wide area network) connection to the home router, the router itself (the IPv6 Transition CE Router), and the local area networks (LANs) inside the home. Some hosts on the LANs speak only IPv4, some speak only IPv6, and some speak both. Regardless of what is on the LAN side, the router must present both IPv4 and IPv6 service to those hosts, even though the WAN side speaks only IPv6.

The router must support a DNS proxy and provide both a graphical user interface and a command-line interface or API for configuring which transition mechanisms to use.
sections.eli5: Picture a router in the middle: the internet side only has IPv6, the home side has devices that need IPv4, IPv6, or both. The router translates between them using special techniques.

sections.title: Five Transition Mechanisms
sections.content:
RFC 8585 requires routers intended for the retail market to support five transition mechanisms, prioritized using a DHCPv6 option. Each mechanism works differently:

464XLAT combines stateless translation on the router (CLAT function) with stateful translation at the ISP (PLAT function). It requires no encapsulation, making it lightweight. The router must support NAT64 prefix discovery.

Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) encapsulates IPv4 packets inside IPv6 tunnels and sends them to a concentrator at the ISP (AFTR), which performs NAT. This shares IPv4 addresses among many customers.

Lightweight 4over6 (lw4o6) extends DS-Lite by moving the NAT function from the ISP concentrator to the home router, reducing centralized state and latency. It requires support for DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 transport.

MAP-E (Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation) uses algorithmic mapping between IPv6 and IPv4 addresses along with IP encapsulation. This allows stateless operation at the ISP side.

MAP-T (Mapping of Address and Port with Translation) uses the same algorithmic mapping as MAP-E but with IPv6-to-IPv4 translation instead of encapsulation, removing tunnel overhead.
sections.eli5: Five different ways a router can translate IPv4 traffic to work on an IPv6-only network. Each works a bit differently: some use translation, some use tunnels, some do stateless mapping. Routers need to support all of them because ISPs might use any one.

sections.title: Configuration and Control
sections.content:
The router must request configuration options for all supported mechanisms via DHCPv6. Initially, all mechanisms are disabled. The router then checks a DHCPv6 priority option (OPTION_S46_PRIORITY) to determine which mechanism to enable. If the priority list matches one of the mechanisms the router supports, that mechanism is enabled. If no match is found and a NAT64 prefix is configured, 464XLAT is automatically enabled. Otherwise, all mechanisms remain disabled until manually configured.

The router must allow administrators to manually enable or disable each mechanism via a graphical interface, command-line interface, or API. For routers serving multiple LAN subnets, different translation rules may apply per subnet, and the router must support this configuration.
sections.eli5: The router asks the ISP which translation method to use, then turns on that one. If the ISP doesn't say, it looks for a NAT64 prefix and enables 464XLAT. Administrators can also manually choose or override the selection.

sections.title: Multicast and UPnP Support
sections.content:
If the ISP provides IPv4 multicast services (such as IPTV), the router must support RFC 8114 for delivering IPv4 multicast to IPv4 clients over an IPv6 network, along with the related DHCPv6 options.

When UPnP WANIPConnection:2 service is enabled but cannot identify available ports, port-mapping requests must be rejected with error code 729. The router may use Port Control Protocol (PCP) or configured port sets to determine availability. All mechanisms must support the Port Control Protocol for advanced port management.
sections.eli5: If your ISP sends TV over the internet as multicast, or you want to run a game server with UPnP port forwarding, the router handles that too.
